title: LLM-Driven Rubric-Based Assessment of Algebraic Competence in Multi-Stage Block Coding Tasks with Design and Field Evaluation
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the challenge of assessing students’ mathematical competence in online learning environments in ways that go beyond checking final answer correctness. The authors focus on algebraic competence in multi-stage tasks involving quadratic equations and block coding, arguing that conventional automated grading systems do not adequately capture students’ reasoning processes, intermediate steps, and alignment with curriculum-based rubric criteria. The study asks whether a large language model (LLM)-driven, rubric-based assessment framework can provide valid, scalable, and process-oriented evaluation of student work in these complex tasks.

The intervention is a web-based assessment platform built on Algeomath that combines rule-based grading with LLM-supported rubric evaluation. Mathematics education experts designed a multi-stage task sequence centered on finding two consecutive natural numbers whose product equals a target value, using symbolic algebra and block-based programming. The system records students’ intermediate submissions, attempts, feedback logs, self-check survey responses, and short reflections. It maps task segments to rubric dimensions spanning Knowledge and Understanding, Procedural Skills, and Values and Attitudes, then uses the LLM to synthesize evidence into rubric-level judgments and feedback. The study also compares LLM-generated rubric scores with expert ratings to examine validity.

The empirical field study involved 42 middle school students from two schools in South Korea during November–December 2024. Students had previously learned quadratic equations, though their prior programming experience varied. Teachers introduced the lesson goals and platform usage, while a teaching assistant provided technical support. Students completed the multi-stage tasks in a guided classroom session, receiving automated formative feedback with up to four attempts per item. Quantitative analyses described score distributions, rubric-wise performance, learner clusters, and agreement between LLM and expert scoring, while open-ended reflections and expert interpretation informed the broader evaluation context.

The main conclusions are that the LLM-based rubric assessment aligned strongly with expert judgments and was able to generate rubric-aligned, process-sensitive evaluations at scale. Students performed relatively well on conceptual and structured tasks but showed weaker performance on more advanced block-coding and proactive tool-use dimensions. The authors conclude that this framework is a promising approach for scalable assessment in mathematics and STEM education, especially where process tracing and rubric-based feedback are important. At the same time, they note that the study is limited by its small sample and narrow problem domain, and they call for future validation with larger datasets and broader content areas.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A large language model used as a rubric-aligned assessment engine to evaluate open-ended mathematical reasoning, coding-related work, and holistic achievement evidence in an online learning platform.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper studies an unnamed LLM embedded in the Algeomath-based platform to score open-ended explanations, synthesize segment-level evidence into rubric ratings across algebra and block-coding competencies, and generate process-oriented feedback aligned with expert-defined rubrics.

findings.finding_summary: In a field study with 42 middle school students, LLM-derived rubric scores showed strong agreement with expert-assigned ratings across five rubric dimensions. Reported alignment metrics were Pearson r=0.79 and Spearman ρ=0.76 (both p<0.001), with average bias M=5.1 points, MAE=12.4, and RMSE=15.8; paired t-tests and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests indicated no systematic divergence beyond a small upward bias in LLM scores.
findings.measure: Agreement between LLM-derived and expert rubric scores across five rubric dimensions
findings.effect_size: r=0.79; ρ=0.76; MAE=12.4; RMSE=15.8; bias M=5.1 points

findings.finding_summary: The study reports that the LLM consistently produced rubric-aligned, process-oriented feedback and that mathematics education experts judged the synthesized evaluations as reducing the cognitive and temporal burden of manual grading. These conclusions are descriptive and supported by the field deployment, but no quantitative time-savings effect size was reported.
findings.measure: Perceived grading scalability and reduction in manual grading burden

quality_tier_rationale: This is an empirical field study with 42 students, but it does not use an RCT or quasi-experimental design to estimate causal effects on student learning. The strongest evidence concerns correlational alignment between LLM and expert scoring rather than intervention impact.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper shows promising validity and operational usefulness of LLM-based assessment, but impact on learning outcomes is unclear and no standardized intervention effect size on achievement is reported.
